articles.title: New UN system platform puts millions of data points at users’ fingertips, says Guterres
articles.summary: How do you make sense of a world facing interconnected crises, from poverty and hunger to climate change, if the facts are scattered across dozens of different places?
articles.content:
The United Nations system is hoping to make that task much easier with the launch of the UN System Data Commons, a new online platform that brings together data and statistics from across the Organization into a single gateway.

Speaking at UN Headquarters in New York on Thursday, Secretary-General António Guterres unveiled the new platform, which allows users to search, explore and access trusted publicly available data from 26 UN entities in one website.

“Behind every statistic is a human story,” the UN chief said, pointing to children whose futures depend on education, families struggling with rising food prices and communities facing growing climate risks.

“To serve them, we must understand their challenges – and know whether we are making a difference,” he said.

One place for trusted information

The platform, available through data.un.org, allows users to search nearly 44 million data points using everyday language rather than navigating multiple websites and databases.

Users can explore trends, compare information across different topics and countries, and trace data back to its original source.

“Access to the knowledge of the United Nations system should never depend on knowing how to navigate its organigramme,” Mr. Guterres said.

The Secretary-General noted that a policymaker often had to look across many different platforms to build a complete picture.

A result of the UN80 Initiative, the new portal removes those barriers by bringing together publicly available data and statistics from the entire UN system in one place.

A tool for the AI age

The launch comes as artificial intelligence is increasingly changing how people find and use information.

Mr. Guterres warned that although people have more information available than ever before, there is often less certainty about what can be trusted.

"If trusted facts are hard to find, unreliable data and misinformation will fill the void," he said.

He stressed that AI-generated answers are only as reliable as the information behind them and said the new platform is designed to help ensure trusted UN system data can be easily found and linked back to its source – by people and digital systems alike.

The website also allows researchers, developers and organizations to connect UN system data directly to their own applications and analytical tools through direct interfaces.

Turning evidence into action

The initiative, known as the UN System Data Commons, brings together public data from 26 UN system entities but does not replace their existing platforms.

Instead, it connects them through a shared gateway, making information easier to discover and access, in accordance with their respective terms of use.

“The UN system produces some of the world's most trusted public data,” said Guy Ryder, Under-Secretary-General for Policy, who added:

“Yet, when that information is dispersed across multiple platforms, its full value is not always realized. The UN System Data Commons now brings this public good into one place, helping people everywhere turn authoritative data into better-informed decisions.”

According to the Secretary-General, the project also demonstrates the goals of the UN80 initiative. It is shared infrastructure – built faster and more efficiently than if each UN organization acts alone.

Calling it “reform people can use,” Mr. Guterres said in his remarks Thursday evening that the value of the new platform would be measured by whether it leads to better support for countries, better-informed decisions and stronger results for people around the world.

“Trusted evidence should not sit behind institutional walls,” he said. “Let us bring it within reach of everyone working for a more peaceful, sustainable and just world.”

articles.title: Exclusive: New evidence for hidden chambers beyond Tutankhamun’s tomb
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02621-2Geophysical survey yields ‘tantalizing’ data that could point to Nefertiti’s burial place – but it’s too early to draw definitive conclusions.
articles.content:
Ancient Egyptian queen Nefertiti, thought to have ruled as Pharaoh, might be buried near Tutankhamun. Credit: Filo/Getty

Tutankhamun’s tomb in Egypt’s Valley of the Kings has long puzzled archaeologists. Might hidden chambers — suspected to hold the remains of Nefertiti — lie beyond its walls? Now, researchers say they have found new evidence pointing to this controversial conclusion.

The decision of whether to peek into the supposed chambers, a few metres from the existing tomb, is in the hands of Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities. If approved, careful drilling to deploy miniature tractors equipped with cameras could start in November, co-author of the study George Ballard told Nature.

The researchers conducted a range of geophysical surveys, including the first use of gravitational techniques to probe the density of ground around the site, as well as ground-penetrating radar (GPR) from inside the tomb. Taken together with studies of the tomb structure, the ground around it and wall paintings, the data strongly suggest that there is a “hidden complex” of corridors and rooms that pre-dates the entombment of Tutankhamun, says lead researcher Mamdouh Eldamaty, an archaeologist at Ain Shams University in Cairo and former antiquities minister of the Egyptian government.

Is this Nefertiti’s tomb? Radar clues reignite debate over hidden chambers

If confirmed, this could “rank among the most transformative archaeological discoveries of the modern era”, he adds. The team’s conclusions are published online today in the Occasional Papers of the Amarna Royal Tombs Project1.

Teasing out data

The study is the latest in a string of attempts to picture what lies behind the walls of the tomb, known as KV62, since co-author Nicholas Reeves, an independent British Egyptologist who has worked extensively in the Valley of the Kings, suggested in 2015 that it could be hiding the resting place of Tutankhamun’s predecessor, Nefertiti. Many Egyptologists think she briefly ruled as a Pharaoh.

The tomb, which was built in the fourteenth century bc and discovered in 1922, is perplexing because it is unexpectedly small for a royal burial. On the basis of lines and cracks in the north wall of the burial chamber, as well as ancient alterations to the room’s paintings, Reeves suggested that the structure was a false wall, of a type often used by ancient Egyptian tomb builders to hide further chambers2.

Reeves proposed that KV62 was originally a much larger royal tomb: when young Tutankhamun died unexpectedly, the entranceway was enlarged and modified for his burial, and the deeper sections were blocked off. But geophysical analyses aiming to test his theory have so far yielded mixed results. Some researchers concluded that chambers were indeed present; others found that the data revealed nothing.

Now, Eldamaty and his colleagues at Egypt’s National Research Institute of Astronomy and Geophysics have once more used GPR to probe the interior walls of the tomb. Ballard, a structural engineer and president of the GBG Group, an international geophysics consultancy, analysed the results, as well as all available data from the previous surveys. Ballard is confident that they show a 2-metre-wide corridor, densely packed with rubble, leading away from the burial chamber. He argues that previous teams missed it because they were looking instead for a large void immediately behind the wall.

GPR, conducted through the walls from inside the tomb, has a limited range, so the team also turned to a microgravity survey — a non-invasive technique that measures density through tiny variations in Earth’s gravitational field — to investigate the area over and around the tomb. Ballard says that the data, from more than 1,200 readings across a 35-square-metre area, show what could be artificial chambers: “structures with right angles, of low density — and those structures are interestingly parallel on their axes to the north wall”. Data collected in 20173 by electrical-resistivity tomography, a technique that maps sub-surface structures, show anomalies in similar locations, although these were dismissed at the time as not being related to KV62.

Ballard highlights one feature, ‘anomaly 7’, as particularly intriguing: a mostly low-density zone hosting a roughly square, high-density area within it. This feature might be a chamber filled with objects, he suggests — although he admits that he is “looking at the very limits of detection”. The proposed chambers do not seem to link to any other entrances, suggesting that — if they exist — they have not been entered since ancient times. A further possible room lies immediately to the west of the burial chamber, although Ballard says the signal here is complicated by the gravitational effect of another tomb that lies nearby.

Other geophysicists are intrigued but cautious. Christopher Gaffney, an archaeologist and GPR specialist at the University of Bradford, UK, describes the report as “fascinating” but says that it doesn’t provide enough information to draw definitive conclusions. “I’m feeling pretty ambivalent,” he says.

From the microgravity data, the presence of chambers “looks plausible”, says Peter Styles, a geophysicist at Keele University, UK. But he, too, would like to see more details. Ballard says he doesn’t yet have permission from the Egyptian authorities to release all of the data.

Egyptologists rejoice

articles.personality_title: New clues suggest hidden chambers near King Tut’s tomb may hold Queen Nefertiti’s burial
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Tutankhamun’s tomb, found in Egypt’s Valley of the Kings in 1922, has puzzled archaeologists because it seems too small for a royal burial. Some experts have long suspected there might be secret rooms hidden behind its walls, possibly containing the tomb of Queen Nefertiti, who may have ruled as Pharaoh before Tutankhamun.

**What happened** – A team of researchers used new technology to study the area around Tutankhamun’s tomb. They combined ground-penetrating radar, which sends signals through walls, with a special gravity survey that measures tiny changes in Earth’s pull to find hidden spaces underground. Their data suggests there could be a series of chambers and corridors just beyond the tomb’s north wall. These hidden spaces might have been blocked off long ago and never opened since.

**Impact** – If these chambers are confirmed, it would be one of the most important archaeological discoveries in recent times. Finding Nefertiti’s burial place would help us better understand ancient Egyptian history and the royal family’s story. The discovery could give new information about how tombs were built and how power was passed between rulers.

**What’s next step** – The Egyptian Supreme Council of Antiquities must decide whether to allow a careful exploration of these possible chambers. If approved, small robotic cameras could be sent in starting in November to take a closer look without damaging the site. This cautious approach is important to protect the tomb and any objects inside.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New scientific surveys have revealed strong signs of hidden chambers near King Tut’s tomb that might hold Queen Nefertiti’s final resting place, offering a chance to uncover a major piece of ancient Egyptian history.
articles.personality_title_fr: De nouveaux indices suggèrent des chambres cachées près du tombeau de Toutânkhamon pouvant contenir la reine Néfertiti
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le tombeau de Toutânkhamon, découvert dans la Vallée des Rois en Égypte en 1922, intrigue les archéologues car il semble trop petit pour une sépulture royale. Certains experts pensent depuis longtemps qu’il pourrait y avoir des pièces secrètes derrière ses murs, abritant peut-être le tombeau de la reine Néfertiti, qui aurait régné comme pharaon avant Toutânkhamon.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une équipe de chercheurs a utilisé de nouvelles technologies pour étudier la zone autour du tombeau de Toutânkhamon. Ils ont combiné un radar pénétrant les murs avec une enquête gravitationnelle mesurant de faibles variations de la gravité terrestre pour détecter des espaces cachés sous terre. Leurs données suggèrent qu’il pourrait y avoir une série de chambres et de couloirs juste derrière le mur nord du tombeau. Ces espaces auraient été bloqués il y a longtemps et jamais ouverts depuis.

**Impact** – Si ces chambres sont confirmées, ce serait l’une des découvertes archéologiques les plus importantes de ces dernières années. Trouver la sépulture de Néfertiti aiderait à mieux comprendre l’histoire de l’Égypte ancienne et la famille royale. Cette découverte pourrait apporter de nouvelles informations sur la construction des tombeaux et la transmission du pouvoir entre souverains.

**Prochaine étape** – Le Conseil suprême des antiquités d’Égypte doit décider d’autoriser ou non une exploration prudente de ces chambres possibles. Si l’autorisation est donnée, de petites caméras robotisées pourraient être envoyées dès novembre pour examiner les lieux sans les endommager. Cette approche soigneuse est essentielle pour protéger le tombeau et les objets qu’il contient.

**Résumé en une phrase** – De nouvelles études scientifiques ont révélé des signes forts de chambres cachées près du tombeau de Toutânkhamon qui pourraient abriter la sépulture de la reine Néfertiti, offrant la possibilité de découvrir un élément majeur de l’histoire de l’Égypte ancienne.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevas pistas sugieren cámaras ocultas cerca de la tumba de Tutankamón que podrían contener el entierro de la reina Nefertiti
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La tumba de Tutankamón, descubierta en el Valle de los Reyes en Egipto en 1922, ha desconcertado a los arqueólogos porque parece demasiado pequeña para una sepultura real. Algunos expertos han sospechado durante mucho tiempo que podría haber habitaciones secretas detrás de sus muros, posiblemente con la tumba de la reina Nefertiti, quien pudo haber gobernado como faraón antes que Tutankamón.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo de investigadores usó nuevas tecnologías para estudiar el área alrededor de la tumba de Tutankamón. Combinando radar que atraviesa paredes con una encuesta de microgravedad que mide pequeños cambios en la gravedad de la Tierra, encontraron indicios de espacios ocultos bajo tierra. Sus datos sugieren que podría haber una serie de cámaras y pasillos justo detrás de la pared norte de la tumba. Estos espacios ocultos podrían haber sido bloqueados hace mucho tiempo y nunca abiertos desde entonces.

**Impacto** – Si se confirman estas cámaras, sería uno de los descubrimientos arqueológicos más importantes de los últimos tiempos. Encontrar el lugar de descanso de Nefertiti ayudaría a entender mejor la historia del antiguo Egipto y la familia real. Este hallazgo podría aportar nueva información sobre cómo se construyeron las tumbas y cómo se transmitió el poder entre gobernantes.

**Próximo paso** – El Consejo Supremo de Antigüedades de Egipto debe decidir si permite explorar cuidadosamente estas posibles cámaras. Si se aprueba, pequeños robots con cámaras podrían ser enviados a partir de noviembre para examinar sin dañar el sitio. Este enfoque cuidadoso es clave para proteger la tumba y sus objetos.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Nuevas investigaciones científicas han mostrado fuertes señales de cámaras ocultas cerca de la tumba de Tutankamón que podrían contener el enterramiento de la reina Nefertiti, ofreciendo la posibilidad de descubrir una parte importante de la historia del antiguo Egipto.
